domanda: Your company plans to deploy an Azure Bastion host that uses the Standard SKU into an existing virtual network. You must create the dedicated subnet that the bastion host will use. What is the minimum subnet prefix that the AzureBastionSubnet must use?
spiegazione: Correct: /26. For any Azure Bastion resource deployed on or after November 2, 2021, the AzureBastionSubnet must be /26 or larger (/25, /24, and so on). A /26 is also the size Microsoft recommends so that host scaling has enough address space for additional scale units. Why the others are wrong: /29 and /28 are far too small and are rejected at deployment; they are the sizes associated with gateway or small workload subnets, not Bastion. /27 was the historical minimum before November 2, 2021 - existing deployments created in a /27 before that date keep working, but a new bastion host cannot be deployed into a /27, which makes /27 the classic trap answer here.

domanda: An administrator wants to connect to an Azure virtual machine through Azure Bastion by running the az network bastion ssh command from the SSH client that is installed on their laptop, instead of using the Azure portal. Which is the lowest Azure Bastion SKU tier that supports this?
spiegazione: Correct: Standard. Native client support (connecting with az network bastion ssh, az network bastion rdp, or az network bastion tunnel) requires the Standard SKU or higher, and the Native Client Support setting must also be selected on the bastion host configuration. Why the others are wrong: Developer is a free shared-infrastructure SKU limited to browser-based connections to one VM at a time and does not support native client. Basic supports only Azure portal browser-based connections; native client, shareable links, IP-based connections, custom ports, and file transfer are all excluded from Basic. Premium does support native client, but the question asks for the lowest SKU that supports it, and Premium adds only session recording and private-only deployment on top of Standard.

domanda: A compliance team requires that every graphical RDP and SSH session made to production virtual machines through the bastion host be recorded and retained for audit. Which Azure Bastion SKU must you deploy?
spiegazione: Correct: Premium. Session recording captures the graphical RDP and SSH sessions made through the bastion host and stores the recordings in a blob container in your storage account via a SAS URL; the feature requires the Bastion Premium SKU. Why the others are wrong: Basic offers only dedicated deployment with two fixed instances and portal-based connections - no session recording. Standard adds native client, shareable links, IP-based connections, custom ports, and host scaling, but session recording is explicitly listed as No for Standard. Developer is the free shared SKU for dev/test and supports one VM connection at a time with no recording capability.

domanda: A key vault named KV1 is accessed by applications that run on virtual machines in VNet1. You create a private endpoint for KV1 that targets the vault subresource, and you plan to create an Azure private DNS zone so that the existing connection strings continue to work. Which private DNS zone name must you create?
spiegazione: Correct: privatelink.vaultcore.azure.net. In the Azure public cloud, the recommended private DNS zone for a Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults private endpoint with the vault subresource is privatelink.vaultcore.azure.net; the public DNS zone forwarders are vault.azure.net and vaultcore.azure.net. Private endpoint DNS zone configurations only generate automatically when the recommended naming scheme is used. Why the others are wrong: privatelink.vault.azure.net looks correct because vault.azure.net is the FQDN suffix users type, but it is a public forwarder, not the privatelink zone name - this is the classic Key Vault mistake. privatelink.keyvault.azure.com and privatelink.vaults.core.windows.net do not exist; the latter borrows the core.windows.net suffix used by Azure Storage.

domanda: You create a private endpoint that targets the sqlServer subresource of an Azure SQL logical server. To integrate the private endpoint with Azure DNS, you must create a private DNS zone that uses the recommended name for the Azure public cloud. Which zone name should you use?
spiegazione: Correct: privatelink.database.windows.net. For a Microsoft.Sql/servers private endpoint using the sqlServer subresource in the Azure public cloud, the recommended private DNS zone is privatelink.database.windows.net, and the public DNS zone forwarder is database.windows.net. Why the others are wrong: privatelink.sql.azuresynapse.net is the correct zone for Azure Synapse Analytics workspaces (Sql and SqlOnDemand subresources), not for Azure SQL Database. privatelink.sqlserver.database.azure.com and privatelink.database.azure.com are invented names - .azure.com is used by services such as Azure Cosmos DB (privatelink.documents.azure.com), but Azure SQL Database uses the database.windows.net suffix. Note also that Azure SQL Managed Instance uses a different pattern: privatelink.{dnsPrefix}.database.windows.net.
tags: private endpoint,private dns zone,azure sql database,privatelink

domanda: Subnet1 in VNet1 hosts several virtual machines that write to a storage account named storage1. You enable the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint on Subnet1 and add a virtual network rule for Subnet1 to the storage1 firewall. From a virtual machine in Subnet1, an administrator runs nslookup against storage1.blob.core.windows.net. What will the name resolution return?
opzione_a: A private IP address from the Subnet1 address range
opzione_b: The public IP address assigned to the storage account
opzione_c: A CNAME to privatelink.blob.core.windows.net that resolves to a private IP address
opzione_d: NXDOMAIN, because public name resolution is removed when a service endpoint is enabled
spiegazione: Correct: the public IP address of the storage account. With service endpoints, DNS entries for Azure services remain as-is and continue to resolve to the public IP addresses assigned to the Azure service. A service endpoint changes routing and the source IP address of the traffic (traffic takes an optimal route over the Azure backbone and the source switches from the VM public IPv4 address to its private IPv4 address), but it never changes DNS. Why the others are wrong: resolving to a private IP address in the subnet is what a private endpoint does, not a service endpoint - a private endpoint injects a NIC with a private IP into your subnet. The privatelink CNAME chain is also created only by Private Link; no privatelink zone is involved with service endpoints. Name resolution does not fail: the public DNS record is untouched, and the storage firewall - not DNS - is what blocks unauthorized callers.

domanda: VNet1 is deployed in the West Europe region and contains a subnet named Subnet1. A general-purpose v2 storage account named storage1 is deployed in the East US region. You must restrict storage1 so that it accepts traffic only from Subnet1, and you must use a virtual network rule rather than a private endpoint. Which service endpoint must you enable on Subnet1?
spiegazione: Correct: Microsoft.Storage.Global. The Azure Storage cross-region service endpoint (Microsoft.Storage.Global) provides connectivity to storage accounts in any region, which is exactly what is needed when the virtual network is in West Europe and the storage account is in East US. Why the others are wrong: Microsoft.Storage is the regional Azure Storage endpoint and provides connectivity only to storage accounts in the same region as the virtual network, so it cannot be used to reach an East US account from a West Europe VNet. Note also that only one of these two endpoint types can be associated with a subnet at a time - if one is already present you must delete it before adding the other. Microsoft.Network is not a service endpoint resource. Microsoft.AzureActiveDirectory is listed under services supporting service endpoints but is used only to support Azure Data Lake Storage Gen1 virtual network integration; Microsoft Entra ID does not natively support service endpoints.

domanda: Subnet2 in VNet1 contains a private endpoint for a storage account and is associated with a network security group named NSG2. You add a deny rule to NSG2 that blocks outbound traffic to the private endpoint IP address on port 443, but virtual machines in VNet1 continue to reach the storage account through the private endpoint. The private endpoint connection is in an Approved state. What should you do first so that NSG2 filters the traffic?
opzione_a: Enable network policies for private endpoints on Subnet2
opzione_b: Add an application security group to the private endpoint network interface
opzione_c: Disable public network access on the storage account
opzione_d: Create a user-defined route for 0.0.0.0/0 on Subnet2 that points to a network virtual appliance
spiegazione: Correct: enable network policies for private endpoints on Subnet2. By default, network policies are disabled for a subnet, which means network security group rules and user-defined routes are not applied to private endpoints in that subnet. To have NSG rules enforced against a private endpoint you must set privateEndpointNetworkPolicies to Enabled or NetworkSecurityGroupEnabled on the subnet; the setting applies to all private endpoints in the subnet. Why the others are wrong: adding an ASG does not help, because ASG support is itself gated behind the same network policies setting. Disabling public network access hardens the storage account's public endpoint but has no effect on traffic that already flows over the private endpoint, which is what you are trying to block. A 0.0.0.0/0 user-defined route cannot override a private endpoint route: the private endpoint propagates a /32 route and, by longest prefix match, the more specific route wins - the documentation explicitly states a 0.0.0.0/0 UDR won't override private endpoint routes.

domanda: A bastion host currently uses the Basic SKU. You are evaluating which capabilities become available only after you upgrade the bastion host to the Standard SKU. Which capabilities require the Standard SKU or higher? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_c: Host scaling to more than two instances
spiegazione: Correct: shareable link, host scaling, and IP-based connection. All three are listed as No for Developer and Basic and Yes for Standard and Premium. Shareable link lets users connect without accessing the Azure portal. Host scaling is available only on Standard and higher and supports 2 to 50 instances, whereas Basic has a fixed count of two instances. IP-based connection lets you target a VM by IP address, including on-premises or non-Azure machines reached over ExpressRoute or VPN, and requires the Standard SKU or higher plus the IP-based connection setting enabled on the Configuration page. Why the others are wrong: Kerberos authentication is supported on every SKU tier, including Developer and Basic, so upgrading is not required for it. Session recording is not a Standard feature at all - it requires the Premium SKU, so it would not become available by upgrading to Standard.
tags: azure bastion,standard sku,host scaling,shareable link,ip-based connection

domanda: Your team is documenting the design constraints that apply to Azure private endpoints before a large rollout. Which statements about private endpoints are true? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: The private endpoint must be deployed in the same region and subscription as the virtual network that hosts it.
opzione_b: The private-link resource can be deployed in a different region than the virtual network and private endpoint.
opzione_c: Clients in an on-premises network can reach the private endpoint over a VPN or ExpressRoute connection.
opzione_d: A single private endpoint on a storage account provides access to both the blob and file subresources.
opzione_e: Private endpoints can be created on general-purpose v1 storage accounts.
spiegazione: Correct: a, b, and c. The private endpoint must be deployed in the same region and subscription as the virtual network, while the private-link resource itself can live in a different region - this is what makes cross-region private connectivity possible. Private endpoints also enable connectivity from the same virtual network, regionally peered virtual networks, globally peered virtual networks, and on-premises environments that use VPN or ExpressRoute. Why the others are wrong: a private endpoint targets one subresource (groupId). For Azure Storage you need separate private endpoints to access the file and blob subresources, because the platform validates network connections and allows only those that reach the specified private-link resource. Private endpoints can be created only on a General Purpose v2 (GPv2) storage account, so general-purpose v1 is not supported.

domanda: Security policy at your company requires a network security group on every subnet, including AzureBastionSubnet. You must add the ingress and egress rules that Azure Bastion requires so that the bastion host stays healthy and can reach the target virtual machines. Which rules are required? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: Inbound TCP 443 from the GatewayManager service tag
opzione_b: Inbound TCP 3389 from the Internet service tag
opzione_c: Inbound ports 8080 and 5701 from the VirtualNetwork service tag to the VirtualNetwork service tag
opzione_d: Outbound TCP 443 to the AzureCloud service tag
opzione_e: Inbound TCP 22 from the Internet service tag
spiegazione: Correct: a, c, and d. AllowGatewayManagerInbound (TCP 443 from GatewayManager) lets the Bastion control plane communicate with the host. AllowBastionHostCommunication (ports 8080 and 5701 from VirtualNetwork to VirtualNetwork) lets the internal components of Azure Bastion communicate with each other. AllowAzureCloudOutbound (TCP 443 to AzureCloud) lets Bastion reach Azure public endpoints to store diagnostics and metering logs. If you apply an NSG to AzureBastionSubnet you must create all the required rules; omitting any of them blocks platform updates and VM connectivity. Why the others are wrong: inbound 3389 and inbound 22 from the Internet are not required on AzureBastionSubnet - the documentation states explicitly that ports 3389 and 22 are not required there. Users reach the bastion host over TLS on port 443 (AllowHttpsInbound), and RDP/SSH on 3389/22 appear as an outbound rule toward the VirtualNetwork tag and as an inbound rule on the target VM subnet, sourced from the AzureBastionSubnet range.

domanda: Fabrikam plans to deploy Azure Bastion into VNet1 so that administrators can connect to servers that run in an on-premises datacenter by specifying the private IP address of each server. The datacenter is connected to VNet1 by an ExpressRoute circuit that uses private peering. Select the appropriate options to complete the deployment requirements.
opzione_a: Minimum Bastion SKU required to connect to an on-premises server by using its private IP address: [Basic | Standard | Premium]
opzione_b: Required public IP address SKU and allocation method for the bastion host: [Basic and Dynamic | Standard and Static | Standard and Dynamic]
spiegazione: Correct: Standard, Standard and Static, /26. IP-based connection - targeting a machine by IP address rather than by Azure Resource Manager resource ID - requires the Standard SKU tier or higher, and the IP-based connection setting must be enabled on the Bastion Configuration page; it supports on-premises servers reached over ExpressRoute private peering or a VPN site-to-site connection. The public IP address used by a bastion host must use the Standard SKU with Static allocation. The AzureBastionSubnet must be /26 or larger for any Bastion resource deployed on or after November 2, 2021. Why the other choices are wrong: Basic does not support IP-based connection; Premium supports it but is not the minimum, since Premium only adds session recording and private-only deployment. Basic public IP SKU and any Dynamic allocation are rejected by Bastion. /29 and /27 are below the current minimum, although pre-November 2021 /27 deployments continue to work. Note also that this design must not use force tunneling or advertise a default route over the ExpressRoute circuit, because IP-based connection requires Bastion to have internet access.

domanda: You are creating private endpoints in the Azure public cloud for a storage account (blob subresource), an Azure SQL logical server (sqlServer subresource), and a key vault (vault subresource). For each private endpoint you must create the Azure private DNS zone that uses the recommended naming scheme so that the DNS zone configuration is generated automatically. Select the correct zone name for each resource.
opzione_a: Private DNS zone for the blob private endpoint: [privatelink.blob.core.windows.net | privatelink.storage.core.windows.net | blob.privatelink.core.windows.net]
opzione_b: Private DNS zone for the Azure SQL Database private endpoint: [privatelink.database.windows.net | privatelink.sql.azuresynapse.net | privatelink.sqlserver.azure.com]
opzione_c: Private DNS zone for the key vault private endpoint: [privatelink.vault.azure.net | privatelink.vaultcore.azure.net | privatelink.keyvault.core.windows.net]
spiegazione: Correct: privatelink.blob.core.windows.net, privatelink.database.windows.net, and privatelink.vaultcore.azure.net. These are the recommended private DNS zone names for the blob, sqlServer, and vault subresources in the Azure public cloud; private endpoint private DNS zone configurations only generate automatically when the recommended naming scheme is used. Why the other choices are wrong: privatelink.storage.core.windows.net and blob.privatelink.core.windows.net invert or invent the storage zone - the pattern is always privatelink prefixed to the public forwarder (blob.core.windows.net). privatelink.sql.azuresynapse.net belongs to Azure Synapse Analytics workspaces, and privatelink.sqlserver.azure.com does not exist. privatelink.vault.azure.net is the most common Key Vault error because vault.azure.net is the FQDN users type, but vault.azure.net and vaultcore.azure.net are the public forwarders while the zone itself is privatelink.vaultcore.azure.net; privatelink.keyvault.core.windows.net does not exist. Remember also that records for multiple services must not be placed in the same DNS zone - create a separate zone per private-link service type.
tags: private endpoint,private dns zone,storage,azure sql database,key vault

domanda: Litware secures a general-purpose v2 storage account named storage1 by setting Public network access to Enabled from selected virtual networks and IP addresses, and by adding a virtual network rule for Subnet1 in VNet1. Both VNet1 and storage1 are in the East US region. An on-premises datacenter connects to Azure by using ExpressRoute with Microsoft peering. Select the appropriate options based on this configuration.
opzione_a: Source IP address that storage1 records for requests from a VM in Subnet1 after the service endpoint is enabled: [The public IPv4 address of the VM | The private IPv4 address of the VM | The public IPv4 address of the virtual network gateway]
opzione_b: Result of resolving storage1.blob.core.windows.net from the VM in Subnet1: [Resolves to a private IP address | Resolves to the public IP address of storage1 | Resolution fails]
opzione_c: Service endpoint resource that must be enabled on Subnet1 if storage1 is later moved to the West US region: [Microsoft.Storage | Microsoft.Storage.Global | Microsoft.Network]
opzione_d: Requirement to allow access to storage1 from the on-premises datacenter: [The existing virtual network rule is sufficient | An IP network rule that allows the ExpressRoute NAT IP addresses | A service endpoint enabled on the on-premises network]
risposta_corretta: The private IPv4 address of the VM,Resolves to the public IP address of storage1,Microsoft.Storage.Global,An IP network rule that allows the ExpressRoute NAT IP addresses
spiegazione: Correct answers explained. Source IP: with service endpoints, service traffic switches from using public IPv4 addresses to using virtual network private addresses as the source IP, which is why any existing storage firewall IP rules based on Azure public IPs stop working after the switch. DNS: DNS entries for Azure services remain as-is and continue to resolve to the public IP addresses assigned to the service - service endpoints change routing, not name resolution. Cross-region: Microsoft.Storage provides connectivity only to storage accounts in the same region as the virtual network, so a move to West US requires the cross-region endpoint Microsoft.Storage.Global, which provides connectivity to storage accounts in any region; only one of the two endpoint types can be associated with a subnet at a time. On-premises: endpoints can't be used for traffic from on-premises services to Azure services. By default, Azure service resources secured to virtual networks aren't reachable from on-premises networks - you must identify the NAT IP addresses used for ExpressRoute Microsoft peering and allow those public IP addresses through an IP network rule in the storage firewall. Why the other choices are wrong: the public IPv4 address of the VM is what storage1 would see without a service endpoint; the gateway public IP is unrelated to intra-VNet service traffic. A private IP resolution result would require a private endpoint, and resolution never fails because the public DNS record is unchanged. Microsoft.Network is not a service endpoint resource. The existing virtual network rule does not cover on-premises traffic, and service endpoints cannot be enabled outside an Azure virtual network.

domanda:
Contoso deploys an Azure Bastion host named Bastion1 that uses the Basic SKU into a virtual network named VNet1. VNet1 is peered with a virtual network named VNet2 that contains several virtual machines. None of the virtual machines has a public IP address. For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.

1. Administrators can use Bastion1 to connect to a virtual machine in VNet2.
2. Administrators can use the az network bastion ssh command on their local computer to connect to a Linux virtual machine through Bastion1.
3. You can configure Bastion1 to use 10 instances to support additional concurrent sessions.
opzione_a: Administrators can use Bastion1 to connect to a virtual machine in VNet2.
opzione_b: Administrators can use the az network bastion ssh command on their local computer to connect to a Linux virtual machine through Bastion1.
opzione_c: You can configure Bastion1 to use 10 instances to support additional concurrent sessions.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - Yes. The Basic SKU supports virtual network peering and connecting to VMs in peered virtual networks. Deploying Bastion once and using virtual network peering to serve multiple networks is a supported design; only the Developer SKU lacks virtual network peering support. Statement 2 - No. Connecting with the native client through az network bastion ssh requires the Standard SKU or higher plus the Native Client Support setting. The Basic SKU supports only Azure portal browser-based connections. Statement 3 - No. Host scaling is available only on Standard and Premium, where you can configure 2 to 50 instances. The Basic SKU has a fixed count of two instances, giving a maximum of 40 concurrent RDP sessions and 80 concurrent SSH sessions (20 RDP and 40 SSH per instance). To scale beyond that you must upgrade the SKU - and note that upgrades are supported while downgrades are not.
tags: azure bastion,basic sku,vnet peering,host scaling,native client

domanda:
VNet1 is deployed in the East US region and contains a subnet named Subnet1 that is associated with a network security group named NSG1. Subnet1 was created by using an ARM template and its network policy settings have not been modified. You create a private endpoint in Subnet1 that targets the blob subresource of a general-purpose v2 storage account named storage1, which is deployed in the West Europe region. An on-premises network is connected to VNet1 by a site-to-site VPN connection. For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.

1. The private endpoint in Subnet1 can connect to storage1 even though storage1 is in a different region than VNet1.
2. A server in the on-premises network can reach storage1 through the private endpoint if DNS resolution returns the private endpoint IP address.
3. By default, the security rules in NSG1 are applied to traffic that is destined for the private endpoint.
opzione_a: The private endpoint in Subnet1 can connect to storage1 even though storage1 is in a different region than VNet1.
opzione_b: A server in the on-premises network can reach storage1 through the private endpoint if DNS resolution returns the private endpoint IP address.
opzione_c: By default, the security rules in NSG1 are applied to traffic that is destined for the private endpoint.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - Yes. The private endpoint must be deployed in the same region and subscription as the virtual network, but the private-link resource can be deployed in a different region than the virtual network and private endpoint. A private endpoint in East US can therefore target a storage account in West Europe. Statement 2 - Yes. Private endpoints enable connectivity from on-premises environments that use VPN or ExpressRoute. The connection works provided name resolution returns the private endpoint IP address, which is why DNS forwarding from on-premises to the Azure private DNS zone privatelink.blob.core.windows.net is the standard requirement in this design. Statement 3 - No. By default, network policies are disabled for a subnet in a virtual network, so NSG rules and user-defined routes are not applied to private endpoints in that subnet. The privateEndpointNetworkPolicies property must be set to Enabled or NetworkSecurityGroupEnabled for NSG1 to filter that traffic. Note that this setting affects only private endpoints - access for other resources in Subnet1 is still controlled by the NSG security rules.

domanda: You must deploy a new Azure Bastion host into an existing virtual network named VNet1 so that an administrator can open an SSH session to a Linux virtual machine by running a command from the SSH client that is installed on a local computer. VNet1 currently contains only a workload subnet. Arrange the four actions in the correct order to meet the requirement.
opzione_a: Run az network bastion ssh from the local computer to connect to the Linux virtual machine.
opzione_b: Create a subnet named AzureBastionSubnet that uses a /26 prefix in VNet1.
opzione_c: Deploy the bastion host by using the Standard SKU and select Native Client Support.
opzione_d: Create a public IP address that uses the Standard SKU and static allocation.
spiegazione: Correct order: b, d, c, a. First create the dedicated subnet named AzureBastionSubnet with a /26 or larger prefix in the same virtual network and resource group as the bastion host; the subnet name must be exactly AzureBastionSubnet and it cannot contain other resources. Next create the public IP address, which must use the Standard SKU with Static allocation - a Basic SKU or dynamically allocated address is rejected. Then deploy the bastion host itself: native client support requires the Standard SKU, and you must select Native Client Support on the Advanced tab at deployment time (or enable it later on the Configuration page). Only after the bastion host exists and native client support is enabled can the administrator run az network bastion ssh from the local computer. The subnet and public IP are prerequisites of the deployment step, so neither can follow it, and the connection command is meaningless until the host is deployed.

domanda: A platform team is standardizing DNS integration for private endpoints across five services in the Azure public cloud, and must create the matching Azure private DNS zone for each one. Arrange the private DNS zone names in the order that corresponds to the following list of private-link resources and subresources: (1) Azure Cosmos DB, Sql subresource; (2) Azure Storage, file subresource; (3) Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2, dfs subresource; (4) Azure Container Registry, registry subresource; (5) Azure Cache for Redis, redisCache subresource.
spiegazione: Correct order: d, b, e, a, c. Azure Cosmos DB with the Sql subresource uses privatelink.documents.azure.com (public forwarder documents.azure.com); the other Cosmos DB APIs use different zones, such as privatelink.mongo.cosmos.azure.com and privatelink.table.cosmos.azure.com. Azure Storage with the file subresource uses privatelink.file.core.windows.net. Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 with the dfs subresource uses privatelink.dfs.core.windows.net - note that Data Lake Storage Gen2 is a storage account resource type, so its zone follows the same core.windows.net pattern but with the dfs suffix rather than blob. Azure Container Registry uses privatelink.azurecr.io. Azure Cache for Redis uses privatelink.redis.cache.windows.net, which must not be confused with privatelink.redisenterprise.cache.azure.net used by Azure Cache for Redis Enterprise or privatelink.redis.azure.net used by Azure Managed Redis. Any other ordering maps a zone to the wrong private-link resource; because private endpoint DNS zone configurations generate automatically only when the recommended naming scheme is used, a mismatched zone silently breaks name resolution to the private endpoint.
tags: private endpoint,private dns zone,cosmos db,container registry,redis,data lake storage
